label: Cottage cheese
comment: Granular, cooked and washed, then dressed with cream: its own route to a fresh cheese.
note: Industrial cottage cheese in North America is often made by direct acidification of cold skimmed milk with food acid (US label: direct acid set) instead of a starter; the cultured route is the main one in the UK and Europe.

about.text: A soft, unripened, rindless cheese of separate, near-white curd grains about 3–12 mm across, made from skimmed milk that is soured, cut and cooked, then usually mixed with a cream dressing.

links.name: Codex Standard for Cottage Cheese, CXS 273-1968

sources.text: The photograph, its author and its licence, from its page.

how.text: Skimmed milk is soured with a mesophilic starter and a drop of rennet, the gel is cut into small cubes and cooked until the grains firm up, then the whey is drained and the grains are washed cold so they do not stay sour. The grains are then mixed with a cream dressing. Washing dilutes the lactose and lactic acid and chilling stops the curd souring further.

steps.note: A mesophilic culture that must not be gassy (heterofermentative) or ropy.
A little rennet, 50 IMCU per 100 kg, is added about 90 min after the culture.
At pH about 4.8, then rested 15–20 min.
Raised 0.5 °C per 5 min for the first 30 min, faster later, over about 2 h; the heat stops the culture.
First of three washes, to wash out lactic acid; Tetra Pak: 30, 16 and 4 °C.
They decide most of the flavour (Tetra Pak: pasteurised cream with a little salt, heated to 80–90 °C, added at 4 °C).

processing.text: Some blends also carry Streptococcus thermophilus. The culture must not be gassy or ropy; rennet goes in about 90 min after it. Industrial North American cottage cheese is often set by direct acid instead.
